Clearly we have made great generalizations in comparing and contrasting the various philosophical movements of these traditions, both in the choices about which materials to include and not to include as well as in the emphases that have been placed on what has been covered. Whatever conclusions are reached here are, of course, qualified by these limitations, and hopefully this will only prompt further debate and dialogue between scholarly and philosophical representatives of all these traditions. Nonetheless, in the great encounters that took place between the ever-transforming thought of Buddhism and South Asian Brāhmiṇical and Chinese Confucian ideas, some very conspicuous themes emerge whose philosophical significance justifies the foregoing investigations and deserves to be explored more fully and fruitfully.

It is certainly true, particularly with regard to the sense organs themselves, that notions of “mirroring” or “transparency” or “construction” of things in our experience are present in many different varieties in classical Asian systems. But these functions or relationships of the powers of the sense organs vis-à-vis the objects of our experience are, in the schools we have covered, clearly distinguished from the more fundamental luminosity of mind. The mind’s luminosity does not simply reflect the world or arrange it according to its own principles but instead does something to nature that could not otherwise be done to it, namely, makes it fully manifest and allows every reach and feature of it, from its most elemental workings to its limitless breadth and duration, to be experienced, appreciated, fathomed, understood, put into words, and used. Now, at the same time, for all that was invested in the notion of mental luminosity and how it could be thought of as the irreducible core of human existence, no school of thought in the spectrum of classical Asian traditions ever denied that our capacity to fully manifest both the world and ourselves in knowing and conduct was crucially dependent on our physical existence and what potentials attended our physicality. In pre-Buddhist Chinese thought, understanding the specifically human bodily configurations of 氣 qi or “vital vapor” and the basic capacities of the heart (心 xin), itself a physical organ, could help us uncover both the original condition of human dispositions and the social and moral ideals toward which we ought to strive. In the South Asian traditions, the notion of karma (rendered into 業 ye in Chinese Buddhist texts) is not merely an abstract moral notion, but is physically created by intentional bodily “actions.” Even in the earliest Vedic texts, karma is frequently referred to as a kind of fine “residue” (anusāya) and “remainders” or “leftovers” of the results of past deeds (karmaphalaśeṣa), making morality very much into a physical matter.2 Of course, in Chinese Buddhist thought, only material 氣 qi combined with material karma and mind could make living bodies also sentient and possessive of certain character traits and moral inclinations. Though medieval Confucians rejected the Buddhist idea that certain desirous inclinations were inherited through karma, they reformulated the early Mencian conviction that moral motives were inborn and looked to a specially delineated conception of 理 li or “natural coherence” to crystallize the scope of our physical, learning, and moral capacities (才 cai). Whether we actually achieve variously idealized states of wisdom and behavior is, of course, contingent on the sincerity and intensity of our personal practice and cultivation. Buddhist views fit within this general framework quite easily, in the sense that they also believed that our natural, physical constitution told a great deal of the story of our present circumstances and ultimate possibilities. However, at least as they thematized the issues, Buddhist philosophers placed enormous emphasis in both South and East Asia on the dynamically complex and yet strictly causal nature of everything that comes about, which includes whatever occurs in the psychological lives of people and how our psychic stores of potentiality enabled the full range of human experiences, from those afflicted with extreme pain to the fully emancipated

In the context of the larger South Asian philosophical tradition, this formulation placed the Vijñānavādins in the position of, on the one hand, denying the Brāhmiṇical assumption that the embodied individual could only be known and freed by a spiritual self that was not of the body and maintaining on the contrary that psychophysical phenomena accounted for everything in our experience. But on the other hand, in the Chinese context, this primordial and invulnerable potentiality for enlightenment, while surely at one with the 氣 qi that makes up the physical heart (心 xin), is, alternatively in Huayen and Chan, thought to be the very causal source (理 li) of the natural order and thus defining of the possibilities of its realization. It was also thought here to be the guarantor that we can slough off all the artificial habits that we have acquired and bring forth a genuineness that the merely impulse-driven body on its own never could. This new vision of the basic perfection of the human mind enabled the Confucian philosophers that followed them to theoretically safeguard the potential for their own moral and social sagehood from any corrupting influence. The Buddhists were, therefore, staunch naturalists, but naturalists with faith or trust (信 xin) that, in its original condition, an original condition that is ever accessible through practice, nature is suffused with perfection.

This will bring us to the concluding mediation, as it were, of the present study. It is a conclusion that is sometimes lost on Western readers, and occasionally is even misjudged by classical and modern Asian thinkers with respect to certain of their own traditions. But, in view of all that we have considered, the conclusion is a fully justified one. With regard to the possibilities of human experience, classical Asian philosophers and practitioners, and surely the Buddhists among them, were incorrigible optimists. They were not, by any stretch of the imagination, naïve optimists.

Buddhist thinkers were not only perhaps more attuned than others to the frailties, ailments, and imperfections of human beings but made great catalogues of and composed innumerable expositions on them. And, despite their high-minded ideals and mythical archetypes of surpassing virtue, Confucians incessantly ran aground on the intractability of ambitious rulers and the shifting tides of history and found themselves objects of sport and derision perhaps more frequently than ones of admiration and emulation, both inside and outside the halls of ritual and ministries. After all, real insight for them revealed that the heart could not be lost. For most of the philosophers we have considered who represented these heritages, when observed and analyzed to its core, human nature was, when traced to its original state, perfect, and so, given enough time and effort, any human being could become perfect.
